opus-5.5.text:
I think it matters a lot, probably more than people expect from the outside.

An open-source project isn't just code sitting on GitHub. It's a set of decisions about what the project is for, what it won't do, and how trade-offs get made. Early on, the founding team holds most of that context in their heads. They know why the scheduler was designed a certain way and why some abstraction looks ugly but exists for a reason. If they step away too early, newcomers tend to either be afraid to change anything or change things without understanding the constraints, and the codebase slowly loses coherence.

The second thing is trust. In a community like vLLM, contributors come from many companies, hardware vendors, model labs, cloud providers, and their interests don't always align. Someone has to be seen as a neutral steward who cares about the project itself rather than any one company's agenda. The founders are often in the best position to play that role, because they built the thing before any commercial interest arrived. When they stay involved, people believe a PR will be judged on its merits.

Third, the pace in AI infrastructure is brutal. A new model architecture comes out and you need support within days. That requires people who can make fast calls with authority, without endless committee discussion. An engaged founding team can do that.

That said, staying involved doesn't mean doing everything yourself. The healthiest pattern I've seen is founders gradually moving from writing most of the code to setting direction, reviewing key designs, and growing new maintainers. If the project depends on a few people forever, that's a failure too. So the goal is for the founders to stay present long enough that the culture and judgment get transferred, so the community can eventually sustain itself. That transition is one of the hardest and most important things an open-source project goes through.

r001.rationale: The response says founders stepping away too early can harm coherence and calls the transition to a self-sustaining community one of the hardest parts of an open-source project, conveying a difficult transition as the core team changes.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it matters a lot, and I say that having watched it from the inside with vLLM.

An open-source project in its early days is really just a few people with a shared picture of what the thing should become. That picture isn't written down anywhere. It's in the founders' heads: why the architecture is shaped the way it is, which trade-offs were deliberate and which were accidents, what the project is for and what it is explicitly not for. When a community grows quickly, you suddenly have hundreds of contributors sending pull requests, each solving their own local problem. Every one of those changes is reasonable on its own. But without someone holding the overall picture, the project drifts. It becomes a pile of features rather than a coherent system.

That's the first role the founding team plays: they're the keepers of taste. Not in a dictatorial sense, but in the sense of being able to say "this is a good idea, but it doesn't belong here" or "we should do this, even though it's painful, because it's the right long-term direction." That judgment is very hard to transfer to someone who joined later, at least not quickly.

The second thing is trust. Companies and individual developers decide to build on top of a project partly based on whether they believe it will still be maintained and still be sane in two years. The founders being visibly active, reviewing code, answering issues, showing up at meetups, is a very strong signal. When founders disappear, even if the code is fine, people get nervous, and forks start to appear.

But I'd add one caveat, because I think it cuts both ways. If the founding team stays involved but never lets go, the community can't actually grow. You end up with a bottleneck where everything waits on two or three people's approval. The healthy pattern I've seen is the founders gradually shifting from writing most of the code to setting direction, building the review and governance process, and deliberately growing new maintainers who they genuinely trust with real decisions. Their involvement changes shape, but it doesn't go away.

So I'd say the ideal is not "founders stay and control everything," and it's also not "founders hand it off and leave." It's founders staying as the anchor for the project's identity while actively building the structures that mean the project no longer depends on them alone. That's a difficult balance, and honestly, most projects get it wrong in one direction or the other.

r001.rationale: The response says founders disappearing can make people nervous and lead to forks, and that founders should gradually change roles. It does not state that a core-team change causes a painful transition period.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s very important, especially in the early stages. The founding team carries a lot of context: why the project exists, why certain decisions were made, and where the difficult problems are. Staying involved helps transfer that knowledge to the community. It also builds confidence that if someone invests time in contributing, there will be people there to review their work and help them move forward.

But staying involved shouldn’t mean controlling every decision forever. Ideally, the founders help other contributors become maintainers and take ownership. To me, success is a community that benefits from the founding team’s participation but can also keep moving when they step back.

r001.rationale: The response discusses founders sharing context and eventually stepping back, but does not say that a change in the core team causes a painful transition period.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s very important, especially in the early stages. The founding team usually has the clearest understanding of why the project exists and what tradeoffs shaped its design. Staying involved helps contributors understand that context and gives them confidence that their work will be reviewed and supported.

But involvement shouldn’t mean controlling every decision forever. Part of the founders’ responsibility is to help other people become maintainers, give them real ownership, and make decisions openly. Ideally, the community benefits from the founding team’s continued participation while becoming strong enough to sustain the project beyond any one person.

r001.rationale: The response discusses founders staying involved and helping others become maintainers, but does not say that changing the core team causes a painful transition period.
